meta.title: Vendor and Third-Party Risk Management Policy

blocks.content: Vendor and Third-Party Risk Management Policy
1. Purpose

The company relies on a growing set of external vendors and service providers across cloud infrastructure, software delivery tooling, payment processing, and customer support operations. This policy establishes a consistent process for assessing, approving, monitoring, and offboarding vendors and other third parties that store, process, transmit, or have logical or physical access to company or customer data, so that engaging a vendor never becomes the weakest link in the company's security and compliance posture.

This policy does not attempt to eliminate vendor risk entirely — outsourcing a capability always means trusting someone else's controls to some degree — but it does insist that the level of trust extended to any given vendor is a deliberate, documented decision proportional to what that vendor can actually touch, rather than an accident of whichever team happened to sign the contract first and how much scrutiny they individually thought to apply.

This policy exists to satisfy the vendor management control objectives of ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A.15 and to give every business unit a single, predictable path to bring on a new vendor without having to invent a risk process from scratch each time. It also gives Legal, Security, and the Data Protection Officer a documented basis for the representations the company makes to customers and auditors about how third-party risk is managed.

The company currently maintains active engagements with several hundred vendors ranging from single-purpose SaaS tools used by one team to infrastructure providers embedded in every production request the company serves. A one-size-fits-all due diligence process would either under-scrutinize the infrastructure providers or bury every small SaaS purchase in weeks of paperwork; the risk-tiering approach in §4 exists specifically to avoid both failure modes.

The cost of getting this wrong is not hypothetical: a majority of publicly reported third-party breaches trace back to a vendor whose access was broader than its actual job required, or whose own security posture was never independently verified before onboarding. A breach that originates in a vendor's environment is still the company's breach in the eyes of its customers and regulators, regardless of whose staff made the mistake, which is why this policy treats vendor risk with the same rigor as an internally owned system rather than as a lesser, outsourced concern.

This policy is reviewed at least annually by the Data Protection Officer and updated whenever a material change in the regulatory environment, a new customer contractual requirement, or a lesson from a past vendor incident warrants it. Changes to the risk-tiering criteria themselves require Change Advisory Board sign-off, since a change that inadvertently downgrades a class of vendor's risk tier could leave existing engagements under-scrutinized without anyone noticing until the next reassessment cycle.
2. Scope

This policy applies to any vendor, subcontractor, managed-service provider, or contractor organization that (a) stores, processes, or transmits company or customer data, (b) is integrated into a production system or pipeline, or (c) is granted logical or physical access to a company facility or system. It covers the full vendor lifecycle: intake and risk tiering, security due diligence, contracting, onboarding, ongoing monitoring and reassessment, incident handling, and offboarding.

The policy is deliberately indifferent to the commercial size of the engagement: a free open-source library maintained by a single volunteer is not in scope merely because the company depends on it (that is a software supply-chain concern governed elsewhere), but a hosted, paid version of that same project that the company sends customer data to for a managed offering is squarely in scope the moment data starts flowing to it. The distinguishing question is always whether the third party receives or can access company or customer data or systems, not how much the company pays it or how the relationship is labeled internally.

Vendors engaged solely for general facilities services, catering, or office supplies, with no data access and no connection to a company system, are out of scope and are handled under standard procurement terms. Any vendor providing an AI or machine-learning-based service that ingests customer data is always in scope regardless of contract size, given the elevated scrutiny such engagements receive from customers and regulators alike.

A vendor that is itself later acquired, or that white-labels a subprocessor the company was not told about at onboarding, remains in scope and must be re-assessed as though it were a new engagement; the risk registry entry is updated to reflect the new corporate structure or subprocessor chain rather than left describing a vendor relationship that no longer exists in the form it was originally approved.

A free trial or proof-of-concept engagement is in scope from the moment any real company or customer data — even a small anonymized sample — is shared with the prospective vendor, not only once a contract is signed. Sales and Engineering teams evaluating a new tool are expected to route the engagement through intake (§4.1) before sharing data, rather than treating a trial period as exempt from this policy because no money has changed hands yet.

Mergers and acquisitions introduce a special case: when the company acquires another business, every vendor relationship the acquired business brings with it is treated as a new, unassessed engagement until Security has had the opportunity to tier and, where warranted, re-negotiate it. Integration plans for an acquisition explicitly budget time for this vendor risk review rather than assuming inherited contracts can simply be renewed on their existing terms.
3. Roles & Responsibilities

Vendor risk management is a shared responsibility between the business owner requesting the engagement, Security, and the Data Protection Officer. No single role can both request and approve a vendor engagement above the Low risk tier, which keeps the tiering decision independent of the commercial pressure to close a deal quickly.

Legal is a required reviewer of the underlying contract for any Critical or High tier engagement but is not itself a risk-tiering decision-maker; Legal's review confirms the data processing terms and right-to-audit clause match what Security and the Data Protection Officer determined was required, not whether the engagement should proceed on business grounds.

rows: Initiates the vendor engagement request and documents the business justification and data flows involved
Performs security due diligence, assigns the vendor's risk tier, and reviews evidence such as SOC 2 reports or penetration test summaries
Reviews and approves the data processing terms and confirms the engagement's data classification is handled correctly
Completes the security questionnaire, supplies evidence of controls, and notifies the company of any security incident affecting company data
Approves onboarding of any vendor assigned a Critical or High risk tier before the engagement goes live
blocks.caption: Table 1. Vendor risk management roles and responsibilities.

blocks.content: 4. Procedure

Every prospective vendor is assigned one of four risk tiers — Critical, High, Medium, or Low — based on the sensitivity of the data it will handle and the depth of its system access. The tier determines how much due diligence is required before onboarding and how often the vendor is reassessed afterward.

rows: Restricted data, or embedded in production request path for a Tier 1 system
SOC 2 Type II or equivalent, penetration test summary, right-to-audit clause, DPO sign-off
Confidential data, or integrated into a production system without direct customer request path
SOC 2 Type II or equivalent, security questionnaire, DPO sign-off
Internal-use data only, limited system integration
No data access beyond vendor's own invoicing/contact details
blocks.caption: Table 2. Vendor risk tier definitions and reassessment cadence.

blocks.content: 4.1 Intake and Risk Tiering

A vendor engagement begins with an intake request from the sponsoring Product Manager, describing the service, the data it will touch, and whether it will connect to any production system. Security Engineering uses the data classification of anything the vendor will handle (see §5) to propose an initial tier, then asks the vendor to complete a standard security questionnaire covering encryption, access controls, incident history, and subprocessor use.

Critical and High tier vendors must additionally supply a current SOC 2 Type II report or equivalent independent audit, and any known material findings from it must be reviewed and either remediated or formally risk-accepted by the Data Protection Officer before onboarding proceeds.
4.2 Ongoing Monitoring and Reassessment

Every onboarded vendor is entered into the vendor risk registry with its tier, renewal date, and next reassessment date. Critical tier vendors are reassessed quarterly, High tier semi-annually, Medium tier annually, and Low tier only at contract renewal. Reassessment repeats the questionnaire and audit-evidence review at a scope proportional to the tier.

A vendor that misses two consecutive reassessment windows is automatically flagged to the Data Protection Officer, who decides whether to suspend new data flows to that vendor until the reassessment is complete. This prevents risk tiering from silently going stale as a vendor relationship ages.

A vendor's tier can also change between scheduled reassessments if the nature of the engagement changes — for example, a Medium tier analytics vendor that is later integrated with a production data pipeline handling Confidential data is re-tiered to at least High the moment that integration is proposed, not at the next annual reassessment date. The Product Manager sponsoring the expanded integration is responsible for flagging the change to Security Engineering before the integration goes live, the same way a new engagement would be flagged at intake.
4.3 Incident and Breach Notification

The vendor security questionnaire and the resulting contract require the vendor to notify the company within 24 hours of discovering any incident that may have affected company or customer data, regardless of whether the vendor has confirmed a breach. Security Engineering triages the notification the same way it would an internally reported incident.

If the affected vendor supports a system classified as critical to service availability, the notification also triggers an assessment under the Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery Policy (POL-009), §4, to determine whether a failover or manual workaround is warranted while the vendor's own incident is contained.

A vendor's contractual 24-hour notification obligation is a floor, not a target: Security Engineering does not wait for the formal notification if it independently detects anomalous activity consistent with a vendor-side compromise, such as unexpected API traffic patterns from a vendor's integration or a spike in failed authentication attempts against a vendor-facing account. Detecting a vendor incident before the vendor discloses it is treated as a success of the company's own monitoring, not a failure of the vendor relationship, and does not change the vendor's own notification obligation once it does become aware.
4.4 Offboarding

When a vendor engagement ends, Security Engineering revokes the vendor's system access within one business day and confirms, in writing, that the vendor has returned or securely destroyed any company data in its possession, consistent with the retention and disposal requirements of the Data Classification and Handling Policy (POL-007), §4.

The vendor risk registry entry is marked offboarded rather than deleted, so that a future re-engagement with the same vendor can reference its prior risk history instead of starting the assessment from zero.

Offboarding is not always initiated by the company; a vendor can also terminate its side of the relationship, whether for commercial reasons, a change in its own business focus, or a decision to exit a market. A vendor-initiated termination follows the same access-revocation and data-return checklist as a company-initiated offboarding, but with a shorter internal notice window in practice, so the sponsoring Product Manager is expected to identify a migration path for any dependent system before the vendor's own wind-down date rather than after it.
4.5 Contractual Requirements and Right to Audit

Every contract with a Critical or High tier vendor includes a right-to-audit clause allowing the company, or an independent auditor acting on its behalf, to request evidence of the vendor's security controls beyond what is volunteered during the standard reassessment cycle. This clause is negotiated by Legal but its inclusion is a hard requirement of this policy, not an optional negotiating point Procurement can trade away to close a deal faster.

In practice, the right-to-audit clause is exercised far less often than it is negotiated: most reassessments are satisfied by the vendor's existing SOC 2 report and questionnaire responses, and a full independent audit is reserved for a Critical tier vendor with an unresolved finding, a vendor supporting a system undergoing its own external certification, or a vendor where a customer contractually requires evidence of direct audit rights before the company can onboard that customer. Exercising the clause without one of these triggers is treated as disproportionate to the risk and is discouraged, since it consumes both the company's and the vendor's limited audit capacity.

Contracts also require the vendor to flow down equivalent data-handling and breach-notification obligations to any of its own subprocessors that will touch company data, so that the company's risk exposure does not silently extend one layer further down the supply chain than what was actually assessed at onboarding.
4.6 Subprocessor and Fourth-Party Risk

A Critical or High tier vendor must disclose its full subprocessor list at onboarding and notify the company at least 30 days before adding a new subprocessor that will touch company data. Security Engineering reviews each disclosed subprocessor against the same data-sensitivity criteria used to tier the primary vendor; a subprocessor that would independently qualify as Critical tier triggers the same due-diligence bar as if the company had contracted with it directly, even though the commercial relationship runs through the primary vendor.

In practice this most often surfaces with cloud-based SaaS vendors that themselves run on a hyperscale cloud provider and use a handful of common sub-processing services for email delivery, analytics, or customer support tooling. The company maintains a pre-approved list of well-known fourth parties whose own security posture Security Engineering has already evaluated once, so that a vendor disclosing 'uses the same email delivery provider as everyone else' does not trigger a redundant full review each time.
4.7 Cloud Infrastructure and Platform Providers

Vendors that host or run production infrastructure directly — cloud compute, managed database, or content delivery providers — are always tiered Critical regardless of the specific data they handle, because an outage or breach at this layer has the broadest possible blast radius across every product the company operates. Onboarding a new infrastructure provider additionally requires an architecture review by Site Reliability Engineering to confirm the integration does not create an undocumented single point of failure.

Because switching a foundational infrastructure provider is rarely realistic on short notice, the ongoing monitoring obligation for this category leans more heavily on continuous evidence — the provider's own public status history, its compliance certifications, and its incident communications — than on the ability to walk away from the relationship quickly if something goes wrong. Where a viable alternative exists, Site Reliability Engineering documents it as part of the vendor's risk registry entry, even if switching is not planned, so that the option is not being evaluated for the first time during an actual outage.
4.8 Vendor Risk Register and Executive Reporting

The Data Protection Officer produces a quarterly summary of the vendor risk registry for the executive team and, where relevant, the Board — the count of vendors per tier, any overdue reassessments, any risk-acceptance decisions made outside the standard tiering criteria, and any Critical-tier vendor incidents from the quarter. This is the same registry, not a separate reporting artifact assembled after the fact, so the numbers presented to leadership always match what an auditor would find if they queried the registry directly.

A risk-acceptance decision — approving an engagement or a renewal despite an unresolved finding from due diligence — is always time-boxed and requires the Data Protection Officer's written sign-off; it is logged in the registry as an explicit exception rather than silently absorbed into the vendor's overall risk rating, so that the underlying finding remains visible at the next reassessment instead of disappearing once someone has decided to accept it once.
4.9 Payment and Financial Data Processors

A vendor that stores, processes, or transmits cardholder data on the company's behalf — a payment processor, a billing platform, or any tool that touches raw card numbers rather than a tokenized reference — is always tiered Critical and must additionally provide current evidence of PCI DSS v4.0 compliance (https://www.pcisecuritystandards.org/document_library/) appropriate to its role in the payment flow, alongside the standard SOC 2 evidence required at that tier.

Where technically feasible, Engineering is expected to integrate with such vendors in a way that keeps raw cardholder data out of company systems entirely, using the vendor's own tokenization or hosted-fields capability; this does not remove the vendor from Critical tier, but it does reduce the company's own PCI DSS scope, which the Security Engineer documents in the vendor's risk registry entry as part of the tiering rationale.
4.10 Vendor Security Incidents Requiring Customer Notification

Not every vendor incident reaches the bar of a customer-notifiable event, but when a vendor incident is confirmed to have exposed company customer data, the notification obligations run on the same timeline and through the same channel as an incident that originated inside the company's own systems — customers are not told a different story depending on which side of a vendor boundary the root cause happened to fall on. The Data Protection Officer and Legal jointly decide notification scope and timing, informed by the vendor's own disclosure but not bound to wait for the vendor's own investigation to conclude if the company's own exposure is already clear.

A vendor incident significant enough to trigger customer notification is always escalated to the Change Advisory Board's next session regardless of whether any code or infrastructure change is involved, since the resulting corrective actions — tightening a data-sharing scope, adding a contractual control, or in the most severe case ending the engagement — are exactly the kind of decision this policy reserves for that forum rather than for Security acting alone.
5. References
Data Classification and Handling Policy (POL-007), §4 — determines the data sensitivity tier that drives a vendor's risk tier and its data return/destruction obligations on offboarding.
Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery Policy (POL-009), §4 — governs the response when a critical vendor's incident threatens service availability.

Software Change Management Policy (POL-001), §4 — any code or configuration change delivered by a vendor into a production system still passes through the standard change process, and a vendor is never a substitute for that policy's approval chain simply because the change originated outside the company.

Related internal artifacts: the service criticality register referenced in the Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery Policy is the same register used to determine whether an infrastructure vendor's role qualifies it for the Critical tier under §4.7; the two registries are kept in sync by Site Reliability Engineering and Security Engineering jointly.

External standards: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (https://www.iso.org/standard/27001), Annex A.15 supplier relationships controls; SOC 2 (AICPA Trust Services Criteria) (https://www.aicpa-cima.com/topic/audit-assurance/audit-and-assurance-greater-than-soc-2), the audit framework this policy accepts as evidence of a vendor's control environment; PCI DSS v4.0 (https://www.pcisecuritystandards.org/document_library/), required additionally of any vendor handling cardholder data per §4.9.

The vendor risk registry, the security questionnaire template, and the standard data processing agreement referenced throughout this policy are maintained by Security Engineering and Legal respectively, and are available on the internal policy portal; this document defines the process and accountability, not the specific wording of those artifacts, which are expected to be revised more frequently than this policy itself.
